newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Multi-million-dollar gassy bubble growing again.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Multi-million-dollar gassy bubble growing again.

text.p: A price bubble is growing again in the multi-million-dollar world market for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and traders in this arcane business expect it to burst early next year.

Like Romanian money pyramid schemes, or the great Dutch tulip speculation of the 17th century, traders say the market for Saudi Arabian LPG is being pushed by a few speculators to artificially high levels.
"People are bidding the market up and the price will eventually get to the point where it falls off the cliff," said a London-based LPG trader for a multinational oil company.
"Someone will be then be left holding the baby."
LPG, the collective term for propane and butane, is used for home heating, in industry for making plastics and for cigarette lighters,
One European trader estimated that speculators had pushed prices $20 a tonne above levels which pure supply and demand would dictate.
SIMILAR PRICE BUBBLE DEFLATED EARLIER

Oil majors Texaco Inc and British Petroleum Co Plc decided this year not to renew large supply contracts with Saudi Arabia's state-owned Aramco, after a similar but smaller price bubble deflated in the spring.
"We are in a sort of upwards vicious circle," another trader said. "It is a bluff and it works because there are not many players in the market."
At the heart of the current pricing game lies the contract pricing system introduced two years ago by Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest exporter of LPG.

Most LPG sales to consumers east of the Suez Canal are priced at premiums or discounts to the Saudi state oil company Aramco's contract price (CP,) published monthly, and nearly half of all imports to Japan, by far the world's biggest importer, come from Saudi Arabia.

Aramco loosely works out its CP according to the bids received for its thrice-monthly sales tenders. A trader will bid a high price for these tenders, buying a relatively small amount of oil at a theoretical loss.

But by keeping larger amounts of LPG in storage and bidding high for these small tenders, traders can turn their earlier loss into big profits by boosting the CP, pumping up the value of their stored oil.
Aramco officials said they were not able to comment.

The Saudi CP for propane has risen from $160 per tonne in July to $250 in November, and end-users fear it may reach a record $300 in December. But paradoxically, stock levels have remained high throughout the period as traders cash in on the paper profits.
WARNINGS FROM JAPAN
This has prompted warnings from Japan, which buys well over a million tonnes of LPG a month, that it may let its importers run down their obligatory stockpiles.
"We just can't afford to buy spot cargoes that cost as much as $300," a Japanese buyer said.
The speculators have been particularly successful this year because other factors have helped the rally.

Chinese demand is soaring, Abu Dhabi has reduced its exports by up to 20 percent since April because of technical problems, and Mexico will suck in an extra half a million barrels a month this winter because of a huge explosion at a gas processing plant five months ago.
Traders say Japanese buyers are likely to put up with high prices because security of supply is paramount.
"Unlike some other suppliers, Aramco has always provided us with the volumes of cargoes they promised to provide," one Japan-based trader said last month.

European traders expect the bubble to burst some time next year as the weather warms up and demand falls in the northern hemisphere. Business is then expected to be carried out at discounts to the CP.
"It is a good game for some," a London-based trader said. "But in the summer months its not so funny."
